title: Has anyone found a workflow for PvE FPS level design?
author: no-fishing90
selftext:
I've spent the last two days trying to make an office level for a single-player PvE extraction FPS in Godot using GPT 6.1 sol and 6 astra. After enough revisions and discarded layouts, I'm starting to question how much of the level design I can realistically delegate.

I initially asked for around 100 × 100 metres. Just getting a playable graybox would have been enough; finished art could wait.

Here's how it went:

* The first layouts were too regular, with lots of straight corridors and oversized rooms. Walking around in first person, almost everything felt too big and empty.
* Then subdivided rooms and added properly sized desks, chairs, partitions, and cabinets. That helped with density, but I still wasn't happy with the layout.
* I used a office floor plan from another game as a reference and repeatedly compared the two. Revisions kept swinging between extremes: a few huge rooms, evenly divided little boxes, or so much room-to-room traversal that going anywhere meant passing through a chain of offices. Asking for fewer corridors eventually produced a version with practically no useful corridor network.
* I supplied a real office floor plan. One interpretation stripped away so much detail that it lost what I liked about the reference. Another felt like tracing the reference rather than adapting it into a game level.
* I also tried having the agent research PvE level design before making another layout, and separately experimented with an office layout generator. I still ended up rejecting results. One graybox implementation was bad enough in play that I asked to revert it entirely.

The frustrating part is that the agent can explain the problems quite convincingly. It can discuss sightlines, alternate routes, room sizes, and circulation, then produce another layout with many of the same issues.

We also had versions that passed navigation and gameplay checks. Those checks were useful, but I still didn't want to keep playing the map.

I'm aware that I chose a fairly large starting scope, and my own feedback may be contributing to the back-and-forth. Two days of failed attempts don't prove this is impossible. But I'm struggling to find an iteration process that actually converges. At the moment, I keep testing a result, explaining what feels wrong, and waiting for another substantial revision.

For anyone who's used AI on an actual FPS level:

1. What do you design yourself, and what do you let the agent decide?
2. What does your workflow look like from reference → layout → graybox → playtest? Do you finish one small combat space first, or establish the whole map's structure?
3. How do you give feedback that improves the next version without causing it to overcorrect somewhere else?
4. Has direct editor access and the ability to inspect or play the level helped meaningfully, compared with generating geometry through code?

I'd especially like to hear about levels you've actually walked around and fought enemies in, including attempts that didn't work. Has AI become a useful level design collaborator for you? Where do you still have to take over?

comments.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
comments.body: You are making qualifications on sightlines, circulation, etc, but are you running a zero context model QA on those criteria?

replies.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
replies.body: No problem. QA is huge, and you can have the building agent do self checks as it builds and reiterates. The no context model as a final pass is important because agents always inflate the scores of work they did themselves
